windows.label: Elect COBRA continuation coverage

due.trigger: the later of the day your coverage ended and the day your election notice is dated

windows.detail: The election period must run at least 60 days and may not end earlier than 60 days after the later of the date coverage terminated or the date you were sent the election notice. A plan may allow longer; it may not allow less.

citation.sourceNote: The election period is of at least 60 days' duration and ends not earlier than 60 days after the later of the date coverage terminates or the date of the election notice.

windows.label: Pay the first COBRA premium

due.trigger: the day you made your COBRA election

windows.detail: A plan may not require any premium payment before the 45th day after you elected. That first payment covers every month back to the day coverage was lost, so it is usually the largest single bill in the sequence — worth knowing before the election deadline, not after.

citation.sourceNote: In no event may the plan require the payment of any premium before the day which is 45 days after the day on which the qualified beneficiary made the initial election.

windows.label: Pay each later COBRA premium
windows.detail: A payment counts as timely if it is made within 30 days after the due date, or within any longer period the plan allows. Miss it and coverage ends on the date of the failure — there is no notice requirement before termination.

citation.sourceNote: Payment of any premium is considered timely if made within 30 days after the date due, or within such longer period as applies under the plan.

windows.label: Choose a Marketplace plan after a qualifying life event
windows.detail: Sixty days from the triggering event to select a plan. For a loss of coverage you know is coming, the same 60 days is also available *before* the event, so you can line up new coverage with no gap rather than a month without it.

citation.sourceNote: Unless stated otherwise, a qualified individual or enrollee has 60 days from the date of a triggering event to select a QHP; for a loss of coverage and certain other triggers, 60 days before the event as well.

windows.label: Choose a Marketplace plan for the 2027 benefit year
windows.detail: Open enrollment for the 2027 benefit year runs from November 1, 2026 through January 15, 2027 on HealthCare.gov. Choose a plan by December 15 for coverage that starts January 1; a plan chosen after that starts February 1. You may read that open enrollment now ends in December: a 2025 rule said so, and CMS is not applying it for 2027. A State-based Exchange may set a later end date, so check your own state's marketplace.

citation.sourceDocument: 45 CFR §155.410(e)(4), as CMS applies it for 2027 — CCIIO statement of July 27, 2026
citation.sourceNote: "HHS ... has not altered the dates for the Open Enrollment period contained in 45 CFR 155.410(e)(4), including related flexibilities available to State Exchanges under 45 CFR 155.410(e)(4)(ii) and (iii). Open Enrollment at the Federally-facilitated Marketplace will begin on November 1, 2026 and end on January 15, 2027." The statement follows the District of Maryland's orders in City of Columbus v. Kennedy (June 12, 2026, No. 1:25-cv-2114; July 16, 2026, No. 1:26-cv-2215), which vacated or stayed parts of the 2025 Marketplace Integrity rule and the 2027 payment notice. eCFR still prints §155.410(e)(5) — open enrollment ending by December 31 and lasting at most nine weeks for benefit years from 2027 — because a court order does not edit the Code, which is why this window cites CMS and not the section. This shard said until 2026-10-19 that the January 15 end "does not carry forward"; for 2027 it does. The December 15 / January 1 and February 1 coverage dates are HealthCare.gov's own (healthcare.gov/quick-guide/dates-and-deadlines, read 2026-10-19), the (e)(4)-era schedule in §155.410(f)(3). The government has appealed, so a later year's window may still shorten.

windows.label: Enroll in Medicare Part B when first eligible

due.trigger: the last day of the month you first become eligible

windows.detail: The initial enrollment period is seven months long: the three months before the month you first meet the eligibility requirements, that month, and the three months after. It is counted in calendar months, not days. Missing it can mean waiting for the general enrollment period and paying a late-enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B.

citation.sourceNote: The initial enrollment period is the 7-month period that begins 3 months before the month an individual first meets the eligibility requirements and ends 3 months after that first month of eligibility.

windows.label: Enroll in Medicare Part B during general enrollment
windows.detail: January through March of each calendar year, for anyone who missed their initial enrollment period and has no special enrollment period available.

citation.sourceNote: The general enrollment period is January through March of each calendar year.

windows.label: Enroll in Medicare Part B after employer coverage ends

due.trigger: the last day of the month your employment-based coverage ended

windows.detail: Eight consecutive months, counted from the end of group health coverage based on current employment. Using it avoids the Part B late-enrollment penalty entirely. Note that it runs from the end of *employment-based* coverage — COBRA is not employment-based coverage for this purpose, so the clock does not restart when COBRA ends.

citation.sourceNote: Section 407.20 is the Part B (supplementary medical insurance) special enrollment period, and it takes the SEP's definition — and so its duration — from 42 CFR §406.24(a)(4). §406.24(b)(2) states that the SEP ends on the last day of the eighth consecutive month during which the individual is at no time enrolled in a group health plan or large group health plan by reason of current employment status.

windows.label: Request a Medicaid fair hearing

due.trigger: the date your notice of action was mailed

windows.detail: This is the MOST your state may give you, not a guarantee. The rule requires a reasonable time not exceeding 90 days from the date the notice was mailed, and a state may set a shorter one. Go by the date printed on your own notice, and if it is not printed, ask the agency in writing today.

citation.sourceNote: The agency must allow the applicant or beneficiary a reasonable time, not to exceed 90 days from the date that notice of action is mailed, to request a hearing.

windows.label: Request a SNAP fair hearing

due.trigger: the state agency's action or the loss of benefits

windows.detail: A household must be allowed to request a hearing on any action or loss of benefits in the prior 90 days. Separately, at any time within a certification period a household may request a hearing to dispute its current benefit level.

citation.sourceNote: A household shall be allowed to request a hearing on any action by the State agency or loss of benefits which occurred in the prior 90 days.

windows.label: Appeal a Marketplace eligibility decision

due.trigger: the date of your eligibility determination notice

windows.detail: Ninety days from the date of the notice, and that is the outer edge rather than a guarantee. A State-based Exchange may instead use its state Medicaid agency's timeframe, which can be shorter and is never less than 30 days — so the date on your own notice is the one that governs, not this one.

citation.sourceNote: The Exchange and the appeals entity must allow an appeal request within 90 days of the date of the notice of eligibility determination, or a timeframe consistent with the state Medicaid agency's requirement provided that timeframe is no less than 30 days.

windows.label: Roll over a distribution you were paid

due.trigger: the day you received the distribution

windows.detail: Money paid out of a retirement plan or IRA can still be rolled into another one, tax-free, if the transfer is made within 60 days of the day you received it. After that it is a taxable distribution. The IRS can waive the deadline for hardship, and a few cases get longer, but you cannot count on either.

citation.sourceNote: The rollover rule does not apply "to any transfer of a distribution made after the 60th day following the day on which the distributee received the property distributed." §402(c)(3)(B) lets the Secretary waive the 60-day requirement for hardship.

windows.label: Avoid the Part D late-enrollment penalty

due.trigger: the day your creditable drug coverage ended, if you were eligible for Part D

windows.detail: A penalty attaches if, after your initial enrollment period, you go 63 days or longer in a row eligible for Part D without a drug plan or other creditable coverage. It is added to your Part D premium for as long as you have Part D, so the count matters more than any single month.

citation.sourceNote: A Part D eligible individual must pay the late penalty "if there is a continuous period of 63 days or longer at any time after the end of the individual's initial enrollment period" without Part D or creditable prescription drug coverage. Unamended since 2017 (eCFR version history).

windows.label: Ask Social Security to reconsider an income-related premium

due.trigger: the day you received the notice of the income-related monthly adjustment

windows.detail: If you think the surcharge on your Medicare premium is wrong, you can ask Social Security to reconsider it within 60 days of receiving the notice. A change in your life that lowered your income, such as retiring, is a different request, a new initial determination, and it has no such deadline.

citation.sourceNote: §418.1325: a reconsideration of an income-related monthly adjustment determination uses "the rules in §§ 404.907 through 404.922". §404.909(a)(1): the request is filed "Within 60 days after the date you receive notice of the initial determination". A new initial determination for a life-changing event is §418.1310.

windows.label: Choose a new repayment plan if you repay under ICR, PAYE or SAVE
windows.detail: The income-contingent plans close. A borrower in one must choose the Repayment Assistance Plan, income-based repayment, or another plan the law allows before July 1, 2028. A borrower who does not choose is moved into the Repayment Assistance Plan, or income-based repayment for loans it does not cover, and starts paying under it that day.

citation.sourceNote: §82001(a)(1): the Secretary shall ensure that "before July 1, 2028", each borrower with loans in an income contingent repayment plan under §455(e) selects the Repayment Assistance Plan, the §493C income-based plan, or another §455(d)(1) plan. (a)(3): a borrower who fails to select is enrolled in the Repayment Assistance Plan, or income-based repayment for ineligible loans, and must begin repaying "on July 1, 2028."

windows.label: Dispute a debt in writing

due.trigger: the day you received the collector's validation notice

windows.detail: A debt collector's first notice starts a validation period that ends 30 days after you receive it, and the notice must state the date it treats as the end. Dispute the debt in writing on or before that date. The collector may assume you received the notice five business days after it was sent, so the date printed on the notice is the one to go by.

citation.sourceNote: "Validation period means the period starting on the date that a debt collector provides the validation information ... and ending 30 days after the consumer receives or is assumed to receive the validation information." A collector may assume receipt on any date at least five days, excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays and Sundays, after providing it. §1006.34(c)(3)(i): the notice states "the date that the debt collector will consider the end date of the validation period".

windows.label: Appeal a claim on your Medicare Summary Notice

due.trigger: the day you received your Medicare Summary Notice

windows.detail: To appeal a decision on a claim under Original Medicare, ask for a redetermination within 120 days of receiving the notice. You are presumed to have received it five days after the date printed on it unless you can show otherwise, and a late request can be accepted only for good cause.

citation.sourceNote: "any request for redetermination must be filed within 120 calendar days from the date a party receives the notice of the initial determination"; receipt "will be presumed to be 5 calendar days after the date of the notice", unless there is evidence to the contrary. §405.942(b) extends the time for good cause.

stateSet.label: Appeal an unemployment determination
stateSet.note: Every state sets its own appeal window and they differ widely. Your determination notice states yours — go by that date, and file as soon as you can. No figure is given here because there is no federal one to give.

stateSet.label: Elect state continuation (“mini-COBRA”) coverage
stateSet.note: Most states have their own continuation law for employers too small for federal COBRA, each with its own election window. Your state insurance department can tell you whether one applies and how long you have.

citation.sourceNote: Each window carries its own citation to the section that sets it; this shard-level citation names the set. Every figure was transcribed from the statutory or regulatory text, not from a summary. One distinction the sources make and summaries routinely lose: the Medicaid fair-hearing period is a CEILING on what a state must allow (“reasonable time, not to exceed 90 days”), while the COBRA, SNAP, and Marketplace windows are floors a plan or agency may exceed but not shorten. Rolled to the 2027 benefit year on 2026-10-19. eCFR's version history shows no amendment to §§155.520, 407.14, 407.15, 407.20, 406.24, 431.221 or 273.15 since before this shard was read, and §155.420's last (2026-07-20) predates its reading; the two §155.420 passages quoted here still read word for word. 29 U.S.C. §§1162 and 1165 carry no amendment from the 119th Congress. The one window that changed is open enrollment, where CMS is applying the November 1 - January 15 schedule for 2027 rather than §155.410(e)(5)'s shortened one; see that window's citation. Six windows were added on 2026-10-19 for SPEC-5 (the 60-day rollover, the Part D 63-day gap, IRMAA reconsideration, the student-loan plan transition, debt validation and the Medicare Summary Notice appeal), each read from its section's own text and each a limit on the reader rather than a minimum someone else must allow.
